title: Mechanics I
subject: Physics

cards.prompt: What is Inertial Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An inertial frame is a reference frame in which a free particle moves with constant velocity. Frames moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame are also inertial in Newtonian mechanics.
required_concepts: Force-free motion has constant velocity.
Constant-velocity translations preserve inertial character.
accepted_variants: A frame in which Newton's first law holds.
major_error_concepts: Calling every stationary-looking laboratory frame exactly inertial regardless of acceleration.

cards.prompt: What is Noninertial Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A noninertial frame accelerates or rotates relative to an inertial frame. Newton-form equations written in it require frame-dependent inertial forces in addition to forces from physical interactions.
required_concepts: Acceleration or rotation relative to an inertial frame.
Additional inertial-force terms are needed for Newton-form equations.
accepted_variants: An accelerating reference frame.
major_error_concepts: Treating fictitious forces as new physical interactions between bodies.

cards.prompt: What is Position Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A position vector points from a chosen origin to a particle's location. Its components depend on the coordinate system and can vary with time.
required_concepts: Vector from chosen origin to particle.
Coordinates depend on the reference choice.
accepted_variants: The vector r specifying location relative to an origin.
major_error_concepts: Treating position as independent of the chosen origin.

cards.prompt: What is Displacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Displacement is the change in position vector, delta r = r_final - r_initial. It depends only on the endpoints and differs from the scalar distance traveled along a path.
required_concepts: Final minus initial position.
Displacement is a vector and need not equal path length.
accepted_variants: Endpoint position change.
major_error_concepts: Identifying displacement magnitude with total distance for every trajectory.

cards.prompt: What is Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position, v = dr/dt. It points tangent to the trajectory, and its magnitude is speed.
required_concepts: Time derivative of position.
Speed is the magnitude of velocity.
accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of change of location.
major_error_concepts: Treating speed and velocity as identical vector quantities.

cards.prompt: What is Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a = dv/dt. It can arise from a change in speed, direction, or both; constant speed does not imply zero acceleration.
required_concepts: Derivative of velocity.
Directional change also produces acceleration.
accepted_variants: Instantaneous vector rate of velocity change.
major_error_concepts: Claiming uniform circular motion has zero acceleration because speed is constant.

cards.prompt: What is Tangential Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Tangential acceleration is the component of acceleration along the instantaneous direction of motion. Its signed magnitude is dv/dt for speed v, so it changes speed rather than providing the normal curvature acceleration.
required_concepts: Tangential component changes speed.
Its signed magnitude is the time derivative of speed.
accepted_variants: Acceleration component parallel to the path tangent.
major_error_concepts: Using v squared over radius as the tangential acceleration.

cards.prompt: What is Centripetal Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For motion along a curved path, normal acceleration has magnitude v squared divided by the local radius of curvature and points toward the local center of curvature. In circular motion this is centripetal acceleration, directed toward the circle's center.
required_concepts: Magnitude v squared over radius of curvature.
Direction is inward normal to the trajectory.
accepted_variants: The acceleration needed to change velocity direction.
major_error_concepts: Treating centripetal acceleration as outward.
Calling centripetal force an additional force separate from the actual net inward force.

cards.prompt: What is Angular Position? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Angular position specifies orientation or location around a chosen axis relative to a reference direction. Radian measure satisfies theta = arc length divided by radius for a circular arc.
required_concepts: Angle relative to a chosen reference.
Radian angle equals arc length over radius.
accepted_variants: The rotation coordinate theta about a specified axis.
major_error_concepts: Using an angle without specifying its reference direction or rotation convention.

cards.prompt: What is Angular Velocity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular position. For fixed-axis motion its signed value is omega = d theta/dt; the corresponding vector points along the axis by the right-hand rule.
required_concepts: Time derivative of angle.
Sign or vector direction specifies rotation sense.
accepted_variants: The angular rate omega.
major_error_concepts: Equating angular velocity with tangential speed without the radius factor.

cards.prompt: What is Angular Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity, alpha = d omega/dt. For a point at radius r in fixed-axis rotation, its tangential acceleration is r alpha.
required_concepts: Derivative of angular velocity.
Tangential acceleration equals radius times angular acceleration.
accepted_variants: The angular analogue of linear acceleration.
major_error_concepts: Equating angular acceleration with omega squared.

cards.prompt: What is Inertial Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inertial mass measures a body's resistance to acceleration under a given net force. In Newtonian mechanics with constant mass, a = F_net/m; mass is a scalar property distinct from weight.
required_concepts: Mass sets response to net force.
Mass differs from gravitational force or weight.
accepted_variants: The proportionality between net force and acceleration.
major_error_concepts: Measuring mass in newtons or treating it as location-dependent weight.

cards.prompt: What is Particle Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The particle approximation treats a body's mass as concentrated at one point when its size, shape, and rotation are irrelevant to the question. It does not claim the real body is physically dimensionless.
required_concepts: Ignore size and orientation when they do not affect the modeled motion.
Approximation depends on the question and scale.
accepted_variants: Point-mass model.
major_error_concepts: Using a point-particle model to determine an extended body's rotational inertia.

cards.prompt: What is Center of Mass? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The center of mass is the mass-weighted mean position: R = sum(m_i r_i)/M, with an integral for continuous matter. It can lie outside the material of the object.
required_concepts: Mass-weighted average position.
Need not coincide with a material point or geometric center.
accepted_variants: The location R defined by the first spatial mass moment divided by total mass.
major_error_concepts: Taking an unweighted position average when masses differ.

cards.prompt: What is Rigid Body? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rigid body is an idealization in which distances between all pairs of material points remain constant. It can translate and rotate but cannot deform within the model.
required_concepts: Internal pairwise distances are fixed.
Translation and rotation remain possible.
accepted_variants: An undeformable extended-body model.
major_error_concepts: Confusing rigidity with being fixed in place.

cards.prompt: What is Internal Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Internal forces are interactions between constituents that both belong to the chosen system. Their classification depends on the system boundary; under Newtonian action-reaction assumptions their vector sum cancels in the system's linear-momentum balance.
required_concepts: Both interacting bodies are inside the chosen system.
System choice determines whether a force is internal.
accepted_variants: Forces exchanged among members of the system.
major_error_concepts: Calling a force internal solely because it acts inside the geometric outline of one body.

cards.prompt: What is External Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: External forces are forces exerted on a system by objects outside its chosen boundary. Their vector sum controls the total linear momentum change of that system under ordinary Newtonian assumptions.
required_concepts: Source lies outside the chosen system.
Classification changes when the system boundary changes.
accepted_variants: Forces applied by the environment to the selected system.
major_error_concepts: Including both sides of an internal action-reaction pair in the external force total.

cards.prompt: What is Net Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on the selected body or system. Component signs and directions matter; a nonzero collection of forces can have zero resultant.
required_concepts: Vector sum of forces.
Nonzero individual forces may cancel.
accepted_variants: Resultant force.
major_error_concepts: Adding force magnitudes without their directions.

cards.prompt: What is Weight? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Near Earth's surface, the gravitational force on a mass is approximately m g directed downward, with g treated as locally constant. Weight in this usage means gravitational force and is distinct from a scale's normal-force reading.
required_concepts: Near-surface gravitational force is m g downward.
Distinguish gravity from apparent weight or support force.
accepted_variants: Weight is the local gravitational force.
major_error_concepts: Saying gravitational force vanishes whenever a falling object is weightless on a scale.

cards.prompt: What is Normal Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A normal force is the contact force component perpendicular to a contacting surface. Its magnitude is determined by the constraints and dynamics, and need not equal the body's weight.
required_concepts: Perpendicular contact-force component.
Magnitude follows from the situation, not an automatic equality to m g.
accepted_variants: The surface-normal reaction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming normal force equals weight on every incline or accelerating surface.

cards.prompt: What is Tension? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Tension is a pulling force transmitted along a taut string, cable, or similar connector. An ideal massless string over ideal pulleys is modeled with uniform tension along a continuous segment; real connectors can violate that simplification.
required_concepts: Pulling force along the connector.
Uniform tension requires appropriate idealizations.
accepted_variants: Axial pulling force carried by a taut connector.
major_error_concepts: Making a flexible ideal string push on an attached body.

cards.prompt: What is Static Friction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Static friction is the tangential contact force that prevents impending relative sliding. Its magnitude adjusts as needed up to a bound, usually modeled as |f_s| <= mu_s N, rather than always equaling that maximum.
required_concepts: Opposes impending relative slip.
Magnitude is bounded, not always at the bound.
accepted_variants: Adaptive no-slip contact friction.
major_error_concepts: Setting static friction equal to mu_s N in every resting configuration.

cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Friction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Kinetic friction acts along a sliding contact and opposes relative sliding of the surfaces. A common dry-friction approximation is f_k = mu_k N; the coefficient and adequacy of the model depend on the materials and conditions.
required_concepts: Opposes relative sliding at the contact.
mu_k N is an approximate magnitude model.
accepted_variants: Sliding-contact friction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming friction must oppose the center-of-mass velocity in every reference frame.

cards.prompt: What is Hooke's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In the Hooke-law regime, a spring exerts F = -k x along its deformation coordinate, where x is measured from equilibrium. The negative sign indicates a restoring direction; the linear law is valid only over a limited deformation range.
required_concepts: Force proportional to displacement from equilibrium.
Restoring sign and limited linear regime.
accepted_variants: A linear elastic restoring force.
major_error_concepts: Using total spring length rather than extension from equilibrium as x.

cards.prompt: What is Drag Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Drag is a resistive force associated with motion relative to a surrounding medium. Models such as F = -b v or F = -c |v|v apply in different flow regimes, with v taken relative to the medium.
required_concepts: Resistance depends on relative motion through the medium.
Linear and quadratic speed models have different applicability.
accepted_variants: A model-dependent fluid-resistance force.
major_error_concepts: Using one universal drag formula for every speed, shape, and fluid.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Linear momentum of a Newtonian particle is p = m v. It is a vector and the momentum of a system is the vector sum of its constituents' momenta.
required_concepts: p equals mass times velocity.
System momentum is a vector sum.
accepted_variants: Translational momentum.
major_error_concepts: Equating momentum with the scalar kinetic energy.

cards.prompt: What is Impulse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Impulse is the time integral of a force: J = integral F dt. It is a vector with units of momentum; for constant force it equals F delta t.
required_concepts: Time integral of force.
Direction and sign matter.
accepted_variants: Area under a force-time curve, component by component.
major_error_concepts: Integrating force over displacement to obtain impulse.

cards.prompt: What is Translational Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Translational equilibrium means zero net external force, so the center of mass has zero acceleration. It may be at rest or moving with constant velocity.
required_concepts: Net external force is zero.
Equilibrium does not require zero velocity.
accepted_variants: Force balance.
major_error_concepts: Concluding that zero net force requires the object to be stationary.

cards.prompt: What is Rotational Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Rotational equilibrium means zero net external torque about the relevant fixed origin or axis, so angular momentum does not change. For fixed-axis rotation with constant moment of inertia, angular acceleration is zero.
required_concepts: Net torque is zero.
Constant rotation is compatible with rotational equilibrium.
accepted_variants: Torque balance.
major_error_concepts: Inferring that zero torque always means zero angular velocity.

cards.prompt: What is Work by a Constant Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Work by a constant force over displacement delta r is W = F dot delta r = F delta r cos theta. It measures energy transfer along the displacement and may be positive, negative, or zero.
required_concepts: Dot product of force and displacement.
Only the displacement-parallel force component contributes.
accepted_variants: Force component along motion times displacement.
major_error_concepts: Using force magnitude times path length when the force is perpendicular to motion.

cards.prompt: What is Work by a Variable Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Work by a spatially varying force along a path is W = integral F dot dr. The integral follows the actual path; in one dimension it is the signed area under the force-position curve.
required_concepts: Line integral along the path.
May depend on the path for nonconservative forces.
accepted_variants: Accumulated infinitesimal force-displacement energy transfer.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the line integral by endpoint force times displacement without justification.

cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The translational kinetic energy of a Newtonian particle is K = one-half m v squared. It is nonnegative and depends on the reference frame through speed.
required_concepts: K = m v squared divided by two.
Scalar and frame-dependent.
accepted_variants: Energy associated with particle motion in a specified frame.
major_error_concepts: Assigning negative kinetic energy merely because velocity is negative.

cards.prompt: What is Potential Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A conservative force admits a potential energy U such that its work equals -delta U. Equivalently F = -gradient U where the potential is differentiable; the additive zero of U is arbitrary.
required_concepts: Conservative work equals negative potential-energy change.
Only potential differences matter to the force.
accepted_variants: Energy function whose negative gradient generates the conservative force.
major_error_concepts: Using F = positive gradient U.
Assuming potential energy must always be nonnegative.

cards.prompt: What is Mechanical Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies, E_mech = K + U, for the modeled system. It need not remain constant when nonconservative interactions transfer energy into other forms.
required_concepts: Sum K + U.
Distinguish mechanical-energy conservation from total-energy conservation.
accepted_variants: Kinetic plus conservative-interaction potential energy.
major_error_concepts: Claiming mechanical energy is conserved in every frictional process.

cards.prompt: What is Power? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Power is the rate of energy transfer or work, P = dW/dt. For a force acting on a particle with velocity v, instantaneous mechanical power is F dot v.
required_concepts: Energy transfer per unit time.
Force power is F dot v.
accepted_variants: Rate of doing work.
major_error_concepts: Confusing power with total work or energy.

cards.prompt: What is Torque? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Torque about a chosen origin is tau = r cross F, where r points from that origin to the force's application point. Its magnitude is force times perpendicular lever arm; its direction follows the right-hand rule.
required_concepts: Cross product relative to a specified origin.
Use perpendicular lever arm.
accepted_variants: Moment of a force.
major_error_concepts: Using the full distance as lever arm regardless of force direction.

cards.prompt: What is Moment of Inertia? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Moment of inertia about an axis is I = sum m_i r_perp,i squared, or its continuous integral. It depends on both the mass distribution and the chosen axis and measures resistance to angular acceleration about that axis.
required_concepts: Mass weighted by squared perpendicular distance to the axis.
Axis-dependent.
accepted_variants: Rotational inertia about a specified axis.
major_error_concepts: Treating moment of inertia as a property independent of the axis.

cards.prompt: What is Angular Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A particle's angular momentum about an origin is L = r cross p. A system's angular momentum is the sum of these contributions; for rotation about a fixed principal axis its axial component is I omega.
required_concepts: Origin-dependent cross product r cross p.
I omega is an appropriate axial special case, not an unrestricted vector identity.
accepted_variants: Moment of linear momentum.
major_error_concepts: Assuming L is always parallel to angular velocity for an arbitrary rigid-body rotation.

cards.prompt: What is Rolling without Slipping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Rolling without slipping means the contacting points of the body and surface have zero relative tangential velocity. For a wheel on a stationary surface, the center-of-mass speed is R omega and the instantaneous contact point is at rest in that surface frame.
required_concepts: No relative tangential motion at contact.
v_CM = R omega for a wheel on a stationary surface.
accepted_variants: Pure rolling constraint.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every point on a rolling wheel has speed R omega relative to the ground.

cards.prompt: What is Restoring Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A restoring force points toward a stable equilibrium when the system is displaced nearby. A linear restoring force F = -k x with k positive produces simple harmonic motion for a constant-mass undamped particle.
required_concepts: Opposes displacement from stable equilibrium.
Linear restoring force is a special case.
accepted_variants: Force tending to return the coordinate toward equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every restoring force must be exactly linear at all displacements.

cards.prompt: What is Amplitude? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of displacement from equilibrium in a specified oscillation. For x = A cos(omega t + phi), amplitude is the nonnegative quantity |A|.
required_concepts: Maximum displacement magnitude from equilibrium.
Not the full peak-to-peak excursion.
accepted_variants: Half the peak-to-peak excursion of a symmetric sinusoidal oscillation.
major_error_concepts: Calling the distance from negative peak to positive peak the amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Period T is the time for one complete cycle of periodic motion. For a sinusoid of angular frequency omega, T = 2 pi/omega.
required_concepts: Time per complete cycle.
T = 2 pi/omega for sinusoidal motion.
accepted_variants: Cycle duration.
major_error_concepts: Identifying period with cycles per second.

cards.prompt: What is Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Frequency f is the number of complete cycles per unit time, measured in hertz. It is the reciprocal of period: f = 1/T, while angular frequency is omega = 2 pi f.
required_concepts: Cycles per unit time.
Distinguish f from angular frequency.
accepted_variants: Reciprocal cycle duration.
major_error_concepts: Equating f and omega without the factor 2 pi.

cards.prompt: What is Phase? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Phase specifies a position within an oscillation's cycle. In x = A cos(omega t + phi), the total phase is omega t + phi and phi sets the initial phase relative to the chosen time origin.
required_concepts: Cycle position expressed as an angle.
Initial phase depends on time-origin and coordinate conventions.
accepted_variants: The angular argument of the sinusoidal motion.
major_error_concepts: Confusing initial phase with amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Damping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Damping removes energy from an oscillatory degree of freedom, commonly through a resistive term proportional to velocity. Underdamped motion oscillates with decaying amplitude; sufficiently strong damping can eliminate oscillation.
required_concepts: Dissipation reduces oscillation energy.
Damped motion need not remain oscillatory.
accepted_variants: Decay of free oscillations through energy loss.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all damped motion must oscillate forever at constant amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Driving Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Driving is external forcing applied to an oscillator, often periodically. It supplies or removes energy depending on its phase relative to velocity and can maintain oscillations against damping.
required_concepts: External forcing of the oscillator.
Energy transfer depends on force and velocity phase.
accepted_variants: A driven oscillator receives an imposed time-dependent force.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a periodic drive always increases amplitude without limit.

cards.prompt: What is Universal Gravitation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Newton's universal gravitational force between point masses is attractive, has magnitude G m1 m2/r squared, and acts along the line joining them. The same exterior result applies to spherically symmetric masses treated from outside.
required_concepts: Inverse-square attractive force proportional to both masses.
Separation is between point masses or spherical centers in the appropriate case.
accepted_variants: Newtonian inverse-square gravity.
major_error_concepts: Applying the exterior point-mass formula inside every extended mass distribution without modification.

cards.prompt: What is Gravitational Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Gravitational field g at a point is gravitational force per unit test mass: g = F_grav/m. For a point source M it points toward the source with magnitude G M/r squared.
required_concepts: Force per unit test mass.
Direction toward a positive gravitating point source.
accepted_variants: Gravitational acceleration field.
major_error_concepts: Including the test mass as a multiplicative factor in g.

cards.prompt: What is Gravitational Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Gravitational potential phi is gravitational potential energy per unit test mass. With zero at infinity, a point mass M gives phi = -G M/r, and the gravitational field is -gradient phi.
required_concepts: Potential energy per unit mass.
Point-source potential is negative with zero chosen at infinity.
accepted_variants: Specific gravitational potential energy.
major_error_concepts: Confusing potential with gravitational force or field magnitude.

cards.prompt: What is Escape Speed? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Escape speed is the minimum launch speed needed to reach infinity with zero remaining speed when no additional propulsion or dissipative force acts. From distance r outside a spherical mass M it is sqrt(2 G M/r), independent of test mass.
required_concepts: Marginally unbound trajectory under the specified gravity-only model.
v_escape = sqrt(2 G M/r).
accepted_variants: The speed making total orbital energy zero with potential zero at infinity.
major_error_concepts: Confusing escape speed with the smaller circular-orbit speed.

cards.prompt: What is Constant-Acceleration Kinematics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For constant acceleration, v = v0 + a t and r = r0 + v0 t + one-half a t squared. The equations apply componentwise; the scalar relation v squared = v0 squared + 2 a delta x applies to one-dimensional constant-acceleration motion.
required_concepts: Acceleration must remain constant.
Vector relations can be resolved into components.
accepted_variants: Uniform-acceleration kinematics.
major_error_concepts: Applying the formulas unchanged to time-varying acceleration.

cards.prompt: What is Projectile Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Ideal projectile motion under uniform gravity has constant horizontal velocity and vertical acceleration -g when drag is neglected and axes are chosen horizontally and upward. The components share the same elapsed time even though their accelerations differ.
required_concepts: Horizontal acceleration zero and vertical acceleration -g.
Common time parameter and neglected drag.
accepted_variants: Independent component equations coupled by one flight time.
major_error_concepts: Assuming horizontal velocity vanishes at the top of the trajectory.

cards.prompt: What is Newton's First Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Newton's first law states that in an inertial frame a body with zero net force remains at rest or moves with constant velocity. Sustaining constant velocity does not require a continuing nonzero resultant force.
required_concepts: Zero net force gives constant velocity in an inertial frame.
accepted_variants: The law of inertia.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a moving body requires net force in its direction of travel to keep moving.

cards.prompt: What is Newton's Second Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Newton's second law relates net external force to momentum change: F_net = dp/dt in an inertial frame. For a constant-mass particle this becomes F_net = m a.
required_concepts: Net force changes momentum.
F = m a assumes constant mass and an inertial frame.
accepted_variants: The vector equation of translational dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Equating one arbitrarily chosen force with m a when other forces also act.

cards.prompt: What is Newton's Third Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Newton's third law states that two interacting bodies exert equal-magnitude opposite-direction forces on each other in the elementary Newtonian setting. The pair acts on different bodies, so it does not cancel in a single body's force balance.
required_concepts: Equal and opposite interaction forces.
They act on different bodies.
accepted_variants: Action-reaction force pairing.
major_error_concepts: Pairing a body's weight and its normal force as a third-law pair.

cards.prompt: What is Force Superposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Force superposition means the net force is obtained by vector addition of all applicable interaction forces. Each contribution is resolved in a common coordinate system before combining components.
required_concepts: Vector addition of force contributions.
Use a common coordinate system.
accepted_variants: The resultant is the sum of individual forces.
major_error_concepts: Adding unsigned magnitudes for forces with different directions.

cards.prompt: What is Action–Reaction Pair Boundaries? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An action-reaction pair has one force on each of two interacting bodies. Both cancel when summing internal forces for the combined system, but only one belongs on each body's individual free-body diagram.
required_concepts: One force on each body.
Cancellation depends on choosing the combined system.
accepted_variants: Third-law pairs cannot be cancelled on one body's diagram.
major_error_concepts: Removing an applied force from a single-body diagram because its reaction exists elsewhere.

cards.prompt: What is Friction Direction and Bounds? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Static friction satisfies |f_s| <= mu_s N and opposes impending relative slip; sliding friction is commonly approximated by |f_k| = mu_k N and opposes actual relative slip. Determine the required static force before comparing it with its maximum.
required_concepts: Static inequality versus kinetic approximate equality.
Direction follows relative slip or its tendency.
accepted_variants: Friction selects a tangential contact direction according to slipping behavior.
major_error_concepts: Setting friction opposite acceleration by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Local Spring Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Near a stable equilibrium x0, a smooth force with nonzero restoring slope can be approximated by F(x) approximately -k_eff(x-x0), where k_eff = -F'(x0) is positive. Higher-order terms matter at larger displacements.
required_concepts: Linearize the force about equilibrium.
A negative force slope gives positive restoring stiffness.
accepted_variants: The leading nonzero restoring term is locally Hooke-like when the slope is nonzero.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every stable equilibrium has a nonzero quadratic potential term.

cards.prompt: What is Constraint Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Constraint forces maintain imposed geometric conditions such as fixed string length or contact with a surface. Their allowed directions follow the constraint model: an ideal smooth surface supplies a normal reaction and a taut ideal string pulls along itself.
required_concepts: Geometry determines allowed force directions.
Force magnitude must satisfy dynamics and constraints together.
accepted_variants: Reaction forces enforcing admissible motion.
major_error_concepts: Choosing a convenient constraint-force direction unrelated to the actual surface or connector.

cards.prompt: What is Work–Energy Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The work-energy theorem states that net work on a constant-mass particle equals its kinetic-energy change: W_net = delta K. It includes work by both conservative and nonconservative forces.
required_concepts: Net work equals kinetic-energy change.
All force contributions to work are included.
accepted_variants: The integrated kinetic-energy form of Newton's second law.
major_error_concepts: Equating net work with total mechanical-energy change in every situation.

cards.prompt: What is Mechanical-Energy Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mechanical energy K + U is conserved when all working interactions in the model are conservative and no unaccounted energy transfer crosses the system boundary. Kinetic and potential energy can change individually while their sum remains fixed.
required_concepts: Conservative interactions and appropriate system boundary.
Conserved sum does not require K and U individually constant.
accepted_variants: Delta K + delta U = 0 for the conservative system.
major_error_concepts: Imposing mechanical-energy conservation across a dissipative collision without accounting for internal energy.

cards.prompt: What is Nonconservative Energy Accounting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: When nonconservative forces do work, changes in K + U must be balanced against transfers to other energy forms or across the system boundary. Friction may convert mechanical energy to internal energy without violating total-energy conservation.
required_concepts: Mechanical-energy loss is not destruction of total energy.
Track boundary transfers and internal-energy changes consistently.
accepted_variants: Energy bookkeeping including nonconservative work and thermal effects.
major_error_concepts: Claiming friction violates conservation of energy.

cards.prompt: What is Impulse–Momentum Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The impulse-momentum theorem states that net impulse equals the change in total linear momentum: integral F_net dt = delta p. It remains useful when the detailed time dependence of a brief force is unknown.
required_concepts: Net impulse equals momentum change.
Vector relationship.
accepted_variants: The time-integrated form of the momentum equation.
major_error_concepts: Using a single contact impulse as the net impulse when other appreciable impulses act.

cards.prompt: What is Momentum Conservation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a fixed Newtonian system in an inertial frame, total linear momentum remains constant throughout an interval if the net external force is zero throughout that interval. More generally, the momentum change equals external impulse. Zero impulse over one selected interval guarantees equal initial and final momenta, not constancy at every intermediate time. Internal interactions may redistribute momentum among constituents.
required_concepts: Zero net external force throughout the interval keeps total momentum constant for a fixed system in an inertial frame.
Zero net impulse over only the whole interval guarantees endpoint equality; individual constituents may still change momentum.
accepted_variants: Since dP/dt = F_external,net, P is constant when the external resultant vanishes at every time; equal and opposite impulses at different times only restore the original P afterward.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that canceling external impulses at different times imply momentum never changed in between.
Concluding each constituent's momentum is separately conserved during an isolated collision.

cards.prompt: What is Center-of-Mass Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a constant-total-mass Newtonian system, M a_CM = F_external,net. Internal interactions affect relative motion but cancel in the center-of-mass translational equation under the usual action-reaction assumptions.
required_concepts: Total mass times center-of-mass acceleration equals net external force.
Internal forces do not independently accelerate the system center of mass.
accepted_variants: The center of mass moves as a point particle under the resultant external force.
major_error_concepts: Treating internal muscular forces as sufficient to accelerate an isolated person's center of mass.

cards.prompt: What is Elastic and Inelastic Collisions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy as well as momentum for an isolated system. An inelastic collision does not conserve total kinetic energy; in a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies remain together afterward. Momentum conservation does not require elasticity.
required_concepts: Elasticity refers to kinetic-energy conservation.
Momentum can be conserved in an inelastic collision.
accepted_variants: Collisions are classified by kinetic-energy behavior and, for perfect inelasticity, sticking.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every inelastic collision destroys momentum.

cards.prompt: What is Constant Angular Acceleration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For fixed-axis rotation with constant angular acceleration, omega = omega0 + alpha t and theta = theta0 + omega0 t + one-half alpha t squared. Radian measure is used when connecting angular and linear quantities.
required_concepts: Constant angular acceleration condition.
Angular versions of uniform-acceleration relations.
accepted_variants: Uniform-angular-acceleration kinematics.
major_error_concepts: Using these relations unchanged when alpha varies with time.

cards.prompt: What is Fixed-Axis Rotational Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with constant moment of inertia, the net torque component about that axis equals I alpha. Torques and inertia must refer to the same axis.
required_concepts: Net axial torque equals I alpha.
Fixed axis and constant I.
accepted_variants: Fixed-axis rotational form of Newtonian dynamics.
major_error_concepts: Combining torque about one axis with inertia about another.

cards.prompt: What is Rotational Work? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Work in fixed-axis rotation is W = integral tau_axis d theta. For constant axial torque this is tau delta theta, and instantaneous power is tau omega.
required_concepts: Torque integrated over angular displacement.
Angular displacement uses radians.
accepted_variants: Rotational force-displacement work.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying torque by angular velocity and calling the result work rather than power.

cards.prompt: What is Rotational Kinetic Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The kinetic energy of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis is K_rot = one-half I omega squared. The chosen moment of inertia must be about that axis.
required_concepts: K_rot = I omega squared divided by two.
Inertia and angular speed describe the same rotation axis.
accepted_variants: Energy of fixed-axis rigid-body rotation.
major_error_concepts: Using mass alone in place of moment of inertia.

cards.prompt: What is Angular Impulse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Net angular impulse equals change in angular momentum about a fixed inertial origin: integral tau_external dt = delta L. Zero net external torque therefore conserves angular momentum about that origin.
required_concepts: Torque integrated over time gives angular-momentum change.
Specify the origin used.
accepted_variants: The integrated angular-momentum balance.
major_error_concepts: Inferring angular-momentum conservation about every arbitrary accelerating origin.

cards.prompt: What is Parallel-Axis Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The parallel-axis theorem states I = I_CM + M d squared for an axis parallel to one through the center of mass, with perpendicular separation d. One of the paired axes must be the center-of-mass axis in this form.
required_concepts: I equals I_CM plus M d squared.
Axes parallel, with one through the center of mass.
accepted_variants: The inertia shift formula for a parallel displaced axis.
major_error_concepts: Applying the formula to nonparallel axes.

cards.prompt: What is Kinetic Energy of Rolling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rigid body's total kinetic energy separates into center-of-mass translation and rotation about the center of mass. For planar rolling this is one-half M v_CM squared plus one-half I_CM omega squared; rolling without slipping adds v_CM = R omega.
required_concepts: Add translation and rotation about the center of mass.
Apply the no-slip relation only when it holds.
accepted_variants: Rolling energy is translational plus rotational kinetic energy.
major_error_concepts: Counting only center-of-mass translation for a rolling object.

cards.prompt: What is Mass–Spring Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal mass-spring oscillator with mass m and spring constant k has angular frequency sqrt(k/m) and period T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k). These are amplitude-independent within the linear, undamped model.
required_concepts: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
Linear spring and negligible damping.
accepted_variants: The Hooke-law oscillator period.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the ideal linear spring period increases with amplitude.

cards.prompt: What is Small-Angle Pendulum Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A simple pendulum of length L in uniform gravity has small-angle period T approximately 2 pi sqrt(L/g). The approximation uses sin theta approximately theta with theta in radians; finite amplitudes change the period.
required_concepts: Small-angle period formula.
Point-mass and small-angle approximation.
accepted_variants: The linearized simple-pendulum period.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the same period is exact at arbitrarily large swing amplitudes.

cards.prompt: What is Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In ideal simple harmonic motion, kinetic and quadratic potential energies exchange while their sum remains constant. Speed and kinetic energy are greatest at equilibrium; potential energy is greatest at the turning points.
required_concepts: Conserved total energy with alternating kinetic and potential contributions.
Identify equilibrium and turning-point energy roles.
accepted_variants: Periodic exchange between kinetic and restoring-potential energy.
major_error_concepts: Placing maximum speed at maximum displacement.

cards.prompt: What is Gravitational Potential Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: With gravitational potential energy zero at infinite separation, two point masses have U(r) = -G M m/r. Its increase toward zero with increasing separation corresponds to work required to separate the masses against attraction.
required_concepts: Negative inverse-distance potential with zero at infinity.
Depends on both masses.
accepted_variants: Newtonian gravitational interaction energy.
major_error_concepts: Using the inverse-square dependence of force for potential energy.

cards.prompt: What is Circular Orbital Speed? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a small mass in a circular orbit of radius r around a dominant spherical mass M, gravity supplies the centripetal acceleration, giving v = sqrt(G M/r). The radius is measured from the central mass's center, not from its surface.
required_concepts: Gravity provides v squared/r.
v = sqrt(G M/r) in the dominant-central-mass approximation.
accepted_variants: Circular Keplerian orbital speed.
major_error_concepts: Using orbital altitude directly as r without adding the central body's radius.

cards.prompt: What is Circular Orbital Period? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A circular orbit around a dominant mass M has period T = 2 pi sqrt(r cubed/(G M)), obtained from orbit circumference divided by orbital speed. Thus T squared is proportional to r cubed for the same central mass.
required_concepts: T = 2 pi sqrt(r cubed/(G M)).
Common central mass for the proportionality.
accepted_variants: The circular-orbit form of Kepler's third-law scaling.
major_error_concepts: Claiming period is proportional to radius rather than radius to the three-halves power.

cards.prompt: What is Short-Interaction Momentum Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Impulse and momentum methods are useful for brief interactions when integrated forces are easier to characterize than detailed accelerations. Momentum is approximately conserved during an impact only when the net external impulse is negligible compared with the relevant momentum changes.
required_concepts: Use integrated force effects over the short interval.
Short duration alone does not guarantee negligible external impulse.
accepted_variants: Impact analysis based on impulse balance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every short collision conserves momentum for an arbitrarily selected single body.

cards.prompt: What is Small-Angle Error Scaling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For angles in radians, sin theta = theta - theta cubed/6 plus higher powers. Replacing sin theta by theta has absolute error of order theta cubed and relative error of order theta squared near zero.
required_concepts: Radian-based Taylor approximation.
Distinguish absolute cubic from relative quadratic error scaling.
accepted_variants: The leading fractional small-angle error scales with angle squared.
major_error_concepts: Applying the same coefficients to degree-valued angles.

cards.prompt: What is Neglecting Air Resistance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Neglecting air resistance approximates motion using other dominant forces alone, often gravity. It is useful when drag's effect over the relevant trajectory is small, not simply whenever an object is described as a projectile.
required_concepts: Small dynamical influence of drag is the condition.
Validity depends on speed, shape, medium, and time or distance of travel.
accepted_variants: Drag-free motion is a scale-dependent approximation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming air resistance is automatically negligible for all falling objects.

cards.prompt: What is When Drag Matters? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Drag becomes important when its force or accumulated effect is comparable to the other terms governing motion. For vertical descent, approaching drag-weight balance leads toward terminal speed; the threshold depends on the drag model and object properties.
required_concepts: Compare drag with competing forces or accumulated motion changes.
Terminal descent reflects force balance.
accepted_variants: The drag approximation must be retained when resistance affects the target dynamics appreciably.
major_error_concepts: Treating terminal speed as a universal constant independent of the object and medium.

cards.prompt: What is Limits of Rigidity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The rigid-body approximation fails when deformation changes the behavior being studied. Elastic vibration, bending, impact deformation, or changing mass distribution can make fixed interparticle distances and constant inertia inadequate assumptions.
required_concepts: Deformation matters to the observable of interest.
Rigid-body parameters may cease to describe the dynamics.
accepted_variants: Rigidity is a useful limit, not a claim that real matter never deforms.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all solids are rigid at every time and length scale.

cards.prompt: What is Effective Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For central-force motion with conserved angular momentum magnitude L, radial motion can be described using an effective potential U_eff(r) = U(r) + L squared/(2 m r squared). The second term represents the angular-motion energy in the reduced radial problem.
required_concepts: Central-force reduction with fixed L.
Effective potential includes the positive angular-momentum barrier.
accepted_variants: A one-dimensional radial potential incorporating conserved angular motion.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the effective term as an additional fundamental outward interaction.

cards.prompt: What is Translation Symmetry and Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a standard Lagrangian system, invariance under continuous spatial translations is associated through Noether's theorem with conserved total linear momentum. The symmetry must apply to the full modeled system, not just one part in an external position-dependent field.
required_concepts: Spatial translation symmetry corresponds to momentum conservation.
Symmetry is a property of the full dynamics.
accepted_variants: No preferred absolute position implies the corresponding conserved momentum component under Noether's assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Inferring momentum conservation despite a translation-breaking external potential.

cards.prompt: What is Time Symmetry and Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a standard Lagrangian system, continuous time-translation invariance is associated with conserved energy. An explicitly time-dependent external drive can break this symmetry for the subsystem and exchange energy with it.
required_concepts: Time-translation symmetry corresponds to energy conservation.
External time-dependent driving changes the subsystem accounting.
accepted_variants: Time-independent dynamics admit an associated conserved energy under the usual Noether conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a periodically driven subsystem must conserve its own mechanical energy.

cards.prompt: What is Rotational Symmetry and Angular Momentum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a standard Lagrangian system, continuous rotational symmetry corresponds to conservation of the associated angular-momentum component. Full spatial rotational symmetry gives conservation of the angular-momentum vector under the relevant assumptions.
required_concepts: Rotational invariance gives angular-momentum conservation.
Axis-specific symmetry conserves the corresponding component.
accepted_variants: No preferred rotational orientation implies a Noether angular momentum.
major_error_concepts: Equating symmetry of an object's shape alone with symmetry of all forces acting on it.

cards.prompt: What is Inertial and Accelerating Descriptions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The same motion can be described in inertial or accelerating coordinates. In an accelerating frame, velocity and acceleration transformations introduce inertial terms; including them consistently reproduces the inertial-frame predictions for physical observations.
required_concepts: One physical motion admits different frame descriptions.
Accelerating-frame equations need the appropriate inertial terms.
accepted_variants: Frame changes alter coordinate equations, not the underlying event.
major_error_concepts: Adding fictitious forces in an inertial frame while also keeping the original force equation.

cards.prompt: What is Centrifugal Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a frame rotating with angular velocity Omega, the centrifugal inertial force is -m Omega cross (Omega cross r). It points away from the rotation axis with magnitude m Omega squared times perpendicular distance for uniform rotation.
required_concepts: Outward rotating-frame inertial term.
Not an extra real interaction in the inertial-frame description.
accepted_variants: The outward centrifugal pseudo-force of rotating coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the actual inward centripetal resultant with an outward force in the inertial frame.

cards.prompt: What is Coriolis Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Coriolis inertial force in a frame rotating with angular velocity Omega is -2m Omega cross v_relative. It depends on motion relative to the rotating frame and is perpendicular to that relative velocity.
required_concepts: Velocity-dependent rotating-frame term.
Use velocity relative to the rotating coordinates.
accepted_variants: The Coriolis pseudo-force caused by motion within a rotating frame.
major_error_concepts: Assigning a nonzero Coriolis force to a body at rest in the rotating frame.

cards.prompt: What is Potential Curvature and Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In one-dimensional conservative motion, an equilibrium satisfies U'(x0) = 0. Positive second derivative gives a local potential minimum and local stability; negative second derivative gives instability. Zero curvature requires higher-order analysis.
required_concepts: Equilibrium at zero first derivative.
Positive curvature stable, negative unstable, zero inconclusive.
accepted_variants: Potential minima are locally stable in the conservative one-dimensional setting.
major_error_concepts: Calling every zero-curvature equilibrium stable or unstable without further information.

cards.prompt: What is Dimensional Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dimensional analysis checks whether quantities combined or equated have compatible physical dimensions. It can constrain a relation's form or identify dimensionless groups, but cannot generally determine pure numerical coefficients or prove the physics correct.
required_concepts: Dimensionally compatible terms and equations.
Dimensional consistency is necessary but not sufficient.
accepted_variants: Reasoning with dimensions such as mass, length, and time.
major_error_concepts: Treating a dimensionally correct equation as automatically physically true.

cards.prompt: What is Scaling Arguments? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A scaling argument estimates how an outcome changes when controlling quantities change by comparing powers, dominant terms, or dimensionless ratios. The conclusion depends on maintaining the assumed physical regime and which quantities are held fixed.
required_concepts: Track proportional changes within stated assumptions.
Dominant balance can change between regimes.
accepted_variants: Order-of-magnitude or power-law dependence reasoning.
major_error_concepts: Extending one regime's power-law scaling across a change in dominant forces.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Mechanics I.
